problem.paragraph: Let $$A = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 \end{bmatrix}$$ , and define $$T:\mathbb{R}^{2}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{2}$$ by $$T(\mathbf{x}) = A\mathbf{x}$$ . Find the images under $$T$$ of $$\mathbf{u} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 1 \\ {- 3} \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ and $$\mathbf{v} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} a \\ b \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ .

Let $$A = \begin{bmatrix} .5 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & .5 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & .5 \end{bmatrix}$$ , $$\mathbf{u} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 1 \\ 0 \\ {- 4} \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ , and $$\mathbf{v} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} a \\ b \\ c \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ . Define $$T:\mathbb{R}^{3}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{3}$$ by $$T(\mathbf{x}) = A\mathbf{x}$$ . Find $$T(\mathbf{u})$$ and $$T(\mathbf{v})$$ .

exercise_group.instruction: In Exercises 3–6, with $$T$$ defined by $$T(\mathbf{x}) = A\mathbf{x}$$ , find a vector $$\mathbf{x}$$ whose image under $$T$$ is $$\mathbf{b}$$ , and determine whether $$\mathbf{x}$$ is unique.

problem.paragraph: $$A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & - 2 \\ - 2 & 1 & 6 \\ 3 & - 2 & - 5 \end{bmatrix} , \mathbf{b} = \begin{bmatrix} - 1 \\ 7 \\ - 3 \end{bmatrix}$$
$$A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & - 3 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & - 4 \\ 3 & - 5 & - 9 \end{bmatrix} , \mathbf{b} = \begin{bmatrix} 6 \\ - 7 \\ - 9 \end{bmatrix}$$
$$A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & - 5 & - 7 \\ - 3 & 7 & 5 \end{bmatrix} , \mathbf{b} = \begin{bmatrix} - 2 \\ - 2 \end{bmatrix}$$
$$A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & - 2 & 1 \\ 3 & - 4 & 5 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 \\ - 3 & 5 & - 4 \end{bmatrix} , \mathbf{b} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 9 \\ 3 \\ - 6 \end{bmatrix}$$
Let $$A$$ be a $$6 \times 5$$ matrix. What must $$a$$ and $$b$$ be in order to define $$T:\mathbb{R}^{a}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{b}$$ by $$T \left(\right. \mathbf{x} \left.\right) = A \mathbf{x} ?$$

How many rows and columns must a matrix $$A$$ have in order to define a mapping from $$\mathbb{R}^{4}$$ into $$\mathbb{R}^{5}$$ by the rule $$T \left(\right. \mathbf{x} \left.\right) = A \mathbf{x} ?$$

exercise_group.instruction: For Exercises 9 and 10, find all $$\mathbf{x}$$ in $$\mathbb{R}^{4}$$ that are mapped into the zero vector by the transformation $$\mathbf{x}\mapsto A\mathbf{x}$$ for the given matrix $$A$$ .

problem.paragraph: Let $$\mathbf{b} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} {- 1} \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ , and let $$A$$ be the matrix in Exercise 9. Is $$\mathbf{b}$$ in the range of the linear transformation $$\mathbf{x}\mapsto A{\mathbf{x} \text{?} }$$ Why or why not?

Let $$\mathbf{b} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} {- 1} \\ 3 \\ {- 1} \\ 4 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ , and let $$A$$ be the matrix in Exercise 10. Is $$\mathbf{b}$$ in the range of the linear transformation $$\mathbf{x}\mapsto A{\mathbf{x} \text{?} }$$ Why or why not?

exercise_group.instruction: In Exercises 13–16, use a rectangular coordinate system to plot $$\mathbf{u} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 5 \\ 2 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ , $$\mathbf{v} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} {- 2} \\ 4 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ , and their images under the given transformation $$T$$ . (Make a separate and reasonably large sketch for each exercise.) Describe geometrically what $$T$$ does to each vector $$\mathbf{x}$$ in $$\mathbb{R}^{2}$$ .

problem.paragraph: $$T ( \mathbf{x} ) = \begin{bmatrix} - 1 & 0 \\ 0 & - 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} x_{1} \\ x_{2} \end{bmatrix}$$
$$T ( \mathbf{x} ) = \begin{bmatrix} .5 & 0 \\ 0 & .5 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} x_{1} \\ x_{2} \end{bmatrix}$$
$$T ( \mathbf{x} ) = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} x_{1} \\ x_{2} \end{bmatrix}$$
$$T ( \mathbf{x} ) = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} x_{1} \\ x_{2} \end{bmatrix}$$

Let $$T:\mathbb{R}^{2}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{2}$$ be a linear transformation that maps $$\mathbf{u} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 5 \\ 2 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ into $$\left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 2 \\ 1 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ and maps $$\mathbf{v} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 1 \\ 3 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ into $$\left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} {- 1} \\ 3 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ . Use the fact that $$T$$ is linear to find the images under $$T$$ of $$3\mathbf{u}$$ , $$2\mathbf{v}$$ , and $$3\mathbf{u} + 2\mathbf{v}$$ .

The figure shows vectors $$\mathbf{u}$$ , $$\mathbf{v}$$ , and $$\mathbf{w}$$ , along with the images $$T(\mathbf{u})$$ and $$T(\mathbf{v})$$ under the action of a linear transformation $$T:\mathbb{R}^{2}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{2}$$ . Copy this figure carefully, and draw the image $$T(\mathbf{w})$$ as accurately as possible. [Hint: First, write $$\mathbf{w}$$ as a linear combination of $$\mathbf{u}$$ and $$\mathbf{v}$$ .]

Let $$\mathbf{e}_{1} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 1 \\ 0 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ , $$\mathbf{e}_{2} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 0 \\ 1 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ , $$\mathbf{y}_{1} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 2 \\ 5 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ , and $$\mathbf{y}_{2} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} {- 1} \\ 6 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ , and let $$T:\mathbb{R}^{2}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{2}$$ be a linear transformation that maps $$\mathbf{e}_{1}$$ into $$\mathbf{y}_{1}$$ and maps $$\mathbf{e}_{2}$$ into $$\mathbf{y}_{2}$$ . Find the images of $$\left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 5 \\ {- 3} \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ and $$\left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} x_{1} \\ x_{2} \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ .

Let $$\mathbf{x} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} x_{1} \\ x_{2} \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ , $$\mathbf{v}_{1} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} {- 2} \\ 5 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ , and $$\mathbf{v}_{2} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 7 \\ {- 3} \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ , and let $$T:\mathbb{R}^{2}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{2}$$ be a linear transformation that maps $$\mathbf{x}$$ into $$x_{1}\mathbf{v}_{1} + x_{2}\mathbf{v}_{2}$$ . Find a matrix $$A$$ such that $$T(\mathbf{x})$$ is $$A\mathbf{x}$$ for each $$\mathbf{x}$$ .

exercise_group.instruction: In Exercises 21–30, mark each statement True or False (T/F). Justify each answer.

problem.paragraph: (T/F) A linear transformation is a special type of function.
(T/F) Every matrix transformation is a linear transformation.
(T/F) If $$A$$ is a $$3 \times 5$$ matrix and $$T$$ is a transformation defined by $$T(\mathbf{x}) = A\mathbf{x}$$ , then the domain of $$T$$ is $$\mathbb{R}^{3}$$ .
(T/F) The codomain of the transformation $$\mathbf{x}\mapsto A\mathbf{x}$$ is the set of all linear combinations of the columns of $$A$$ .
(T/F) If $$A$$ is an $$m \times n$$ matrix, then the range of the transformation $$\mathbf{x}\mapsto A\mathbf{x}$$ is $$\mathbb{R}^{m}$$ .

(T/F) If $$T:\mathbb{R}^{n}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{m}$$ is a linear transformation and if $$\mathbf{c}$$ is in $$\mathbb{R}^{m}$$ , then a uniqueness question is “Is $$\mathbf{c}$$ in the range of $$T$$ ?”
(T/F) Every linear transformation is a matrix transformation.
(T/F) A linear transformation preserves the operations of vector addition and scalar multiplication.

(T/F) A transformation $$T$$ is linear if and only if $$T(c_{1}\mathbf{v}_{1} + c_{2}\mathbf{v}_{2}) = c_{1}T(\mathbf{v}_{1}) + c_{2}T(\mathbf{v}_{2})$$ for all $$\mathbf{v}_{1}$$ and $$\mathbf{v}_{2}$$ in the domain of $$T$$ and for all scalars $$c_{1}$$ and $$c_{2}$$ .
(T/F) The superposition principle is a physical description of a linear transformation.

Let $$T:\mathbb{R}^{2}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{2}$$ be the linear transformation that reflects each point through the $$x_{1} \text{-axis}$$ . (See Practice Problem 2.) Make two sketches similar to Figure 6 that illustrate properties (i) and (ii) of a linear transformation.

Suppose vectors $$\mathbf{v}_{1} \text{,…,} \mathbf{v}_{p}$$ span $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ , and let $$T:\mathbb{R}^{n}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ be a linear transformation. Suppose $$T(\mathbf{v}_{i}) = 0$$ for $$i = 1 \text{,…,} p$$ . Show that $$T$$ is the zero transformation. That is, show that if $$\mathbf{x}$$ is any vector in $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ , then $$T(\mathbf{x}) = 0$$ .

Given $$\mathbf{v} \neq 0$$ and $$\mathbf{p}$$ in $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ , the line through $$\mathbf{p}$$ in the direction of $$\mathbf{v}$$ has the parametric equation $$\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{p} + t\mathbf{v}$$ . Show that a linear transformation $$T:\mathbb{R}^{n}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ maps this line onto another line or onto a single point (a degenerate line).

Let $$\mathbf{u}$$ and $$\mathbf{v}$$ be linearly independent vectors in $$\mathbb{R}^{3}$$ , and let $$P$$ be the plane through $$\mathbf{u}$$ , $$\mathbf{v}$$ , and $$0$$ . The parametric equation of $$P$$ is $$\mathbf{x} = s\mathbf{u} + t\mathbf{v}$$ (with $$s$$ , $$t$$ in $$\mathbb{R}$$ ). Show that a linear transformation $$T:\mathbb{R}^{3}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{3}$$ maps $$P$$ onto a plane through $$0$$ , or onto a line through $$0$$ , or onto just the origin in $$\mathbb{R}^{3}$$ . What must be true about $$T(\mathbf{u})$$ and $$T(\mathbf{v})$$ in order for the image of the plane $$P$$ to be a plane?

list.item: Show that the line through vectors $$\mathbf{p}$$ and $$\mathbf{q}$$ in $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ may be written in the parametric form $$\mathbf{x} = (1 - t)\mathbf{p} + t\mathbf{q}$$ . (Refer to the figure with Exercises 25 and 26 in Section 1.5.)

The line segment from $$\mathbf{p}$$ to $$\mathbf{q}$$ is the set of points of the form $$(1 - t)\mathbf{p} + t\mathbf{q}$$ for $$0 \leq t \leq 1$$ (as shown in the figure below). Show that a linear transformation $$T$$ maps this line segment onto a line segment or onto a single point.

problem.paragraph: Let $$\mathbf{u}$$ and $$\mathbf{v}$$ be vectors in $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ . It can be shown that the set $$P$$ of all points in the parallelogram determined by $$\mathbf{u}$$ and $$\mathbf{v}$$ has the form $$a\mathbf{u} + b\mathbf{v}$$ , for $$0 \leq a \leq 1$$ , $$0 \leq b \leq 1$$ . Let $$T:\mathbb{R}^{n}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{m}$$ be a linear transformation. Explain why the image of a point in $$P$$ under the transformation $$T$$ lies in the parallelogram determined by $$T(\mathbf{u})$$ and $$T(\mathbf{v})$$ .
Define $$f:\mathbb{R}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}$$ by $$f(x) = mx + b$$ .

list.item: Show that $$f$$ is a linear transformation when $$b = 0$$ .
Find a property of a linear transformation that is violated when $$b \neq 0$$ .
Why is $$f$$ called a linear function?

problem.paragraph: An affine transformation $$T:\mathbb{R}^{n}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{m}$$ has the form $$T\left( \mathbf{x} \right) = A\mathbf{x} + \mathbf{b}$$ , with $$A$$ an $$m \times n$$ matrix and $$\mathbf{b}$$ in $$\mathbb{R}^{m}$$ . Show that $$T$$ is not a linear transformation when $$\mathbf{b} \neq 0$$ . (Affine transformations are important in computer graphics.)

Let $$T:\mathbb{R}^{n}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{m}$$ be a linear transformation, and let $$\left\{ \mathbf{v}_{1} \text{,} \mathbf{v}_{2} \text{,} \mathbf{v}_{3} \right\}$$ be a linearly dependent set in $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ . Explain why the set $$\left\{ T\left( \mathbf{v}_{1} \right) \text{,} T\left( \mathbf{v}_{2} \right) \text{,} T\left( \mathbf{v}_{3} \right) \right\}$$ is linearly dependent.

image.alt: The figure illustrates a line segment from point p to q with the corresponding equation in parametric form in the parameter t.

exercise_group.instruction: In Exercises 40–44, column vectors are written as rows, such as $$\mathbf{x} = \left( x_{1} \text{,} x_{2} \right)$$ , and $$T(\mathbf{x})$$ is written as $$T\left( x_{1} \text{,} x_{2} \right)$$ .

problem.paragraph: Show that the transformation $$T$$ defined by $$T(x_{1} \text{,} x_{2}) = (4x_{1} - 2x_{2} \text{,} 3|x_{2}|)$$ is not linear.
Show that the transformation $$T$$ defined by $$T(x_{1} \text{,} x_{2}) = (2x_{1} - 3x_{2} \text{,} x_{1} + 4 \text{,} 5x_{2})$$ is not linear.

Let $$T:\mathbb{R}^{n}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{m}$$ be a linear transformation. Show that if $$T$$ maps two linearly independent vectors onto a linearly dependent set, then the equation $$T(\mathbf{x}) = 0$$ has a nontrivial solution. [Hint: Suppose $$\mathbf{u}$$ and $$\mathbf{v}$$ in $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ are linearly independent and yet $$T(\mathbf{u})$$ and $$T(\mathbf{v})$$ are linearly dependent. Then $$c_{1}T(\mathbf{u}) + c_{2}T(\mathbf{v}) = 0$$ for some weights $$c_{1}$$ and $$c_{2}$$ , not both zero. Use this equation.]

Let $$T:\mathbb{R}^{3}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{3}$$ be the transformation that reflects each vector $$\mathbf{x} = (x_{1} \text{,} x_{2} \text{,} x_{3})$$ through the plane $$x_{3} = 0$$ onto $$T\left( \mathbf{x} \right) = \left( x_{1} \text{,} x_{2}, - x_{3} \right)$$ . Show that $$T$$ is a linear transformation. [See Example 4 for ideas.]

Let $$T:\mathbb{R}^{3}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{3}$$ be the transformation that projects each vector $$\mathbf{x} = (x_{1} \text{,} x_{2} \text{,} x_{3})$$ onto the plane $$x_{2} = 0$$ , so $$T(\mathbf{x}) = (x_{1} \text{,} 0 \text{,} x_{3})$$ . Show that $$T$$ is a linear transformation.

exercise_group.instruction: [T] In Exercises 45 and 46, the given matrix determines a linear transformation $$T$$ . Find all $$\mathbf{x}$$ such that $$T(\mathbf{x}) = 0$$ .

problem.paragraph: [T] Let $$\mathbf{b} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 7 \\ 5 \\ 9 \\ 7 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ and let $$A$$ be the matrix in Exercise 45. Is $$\mathbf{b}$$ in the range of the transformation $$\mathbf{x}\mapsto A{\mathbf{x} \text{?} }$$ If so, find an $$\mathbf{x}$$ whose image under the transformation is $$\mathbf{b}$$ .

[T] Let $$\mathbf{b} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} {- 7} \\ {- 7} \\ 13 \\ {- 5} \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ and let $$A$$ be the matrix in Exercise 46. Is $$\mathbf{b}$$ in the range of the transformation $$\mathbf{x}\mapsto A{\mathbf{x} \text{?} }$$ If so, find an $$\mathbf{x}$$ whose image under the transformation is $$\mathbf{b}$$ .
$$A$$ must have five columns for $$A\mathbf{x}$$ to be defined. $$A$$ must have two rows for the codomain of $$T$$ to be $$\mathbb{R}^{2}$$ .

Plot some random points (vectors) on graph paper to see what happens. A point such as $$(4 \text{,} 1)$$ maps into $$\left( 4, - 1 \right)$$ . The transformation $$\mathbf{x}\mapsto A\mathbf{x}$$ reflects points through the $$x \text{-axis}$$ (or $$x_{1} \text{-axis}$$ ).

Let $$\mathbf{x} = t\mathbf{u}$$ for some $$t$$ such that $$0 \leq t \leq 1$$ . Since $$T$$ is linear, $$T\left( t\mathbf{u} \right) = tT\left( \mathbf{u} \right)$$ , which is a point on the line segment between $$0$$ and $$T(\mathbf{u})$$ .
